summary: Deciding whether the information is enough, without solving more than needed.
ideas: The five answers never change: (A) statement 1 alone is sufficient, 2 is not; (B) 2 alone is sufficient, 1 is not; (C) both together are needed; (D) each alone is sufficient; (E) not sufficient even together.
Sufficient means exactly one answer: one value for a value question, always “yes” or always “no” for a yes/no question.
You never need the final number, only to know that one exists.
The two statements never contradict each other.
method: Rephrase the question: what do you really need to know? (“Is x odd?” may become “is x − 1 even?”)
Judge statement 1 alone, then statement 2 alone, forgetting statement 1.
Only if both fail alone, combine them.
Use the grid: if 1 is sufficient, the answer is A or D; if not, B, C or E.
traps: Assuming numbers are integers or positive when the question does not say so.
Carrying information from statement 1 into statement 2.
The C trap: two equations do not always give a unique solution.
Solving completely when a quick check of sufficiency is enough.
shortcuts: To prove “not sufficient”, find two allowed numbers that give different answers.
Test 0, 1, negatives and fractions whenever the question does not rule them out.

example.a: (1) x = 3 or −3: not sufficient. (2) x = 3 only: sufficient. Answer: **B**.

summary: Two linked answers chosen from one shared list of options.
ideas: Each question has two columns and one list of options; you pick one option per column.
The two parts may depend on each other (find one, then derive the other) or be independent.
The same option can be the right answer for both columns.
It can be quantitative (equations, rates) or verbal (strengthen and weaken, cause and effect).
method: Read what each column asks and every condition that links them.
Solve the part with the most constraints first.
Use the options: plug them into the conditions instead of solving from scratch.
Check the pair against every condition before moving on.
traps: Stopping after one part: both must be right to score.
Assuming the two answers must be different.
shortcuts: If the parts are linked by an equation, test options in pairs that satisfy it.

example.q: Choose x and y from 3, 4, 6, 7 and 10 so that x + y = 10 and x − y = 4.
example.a: Adding the equations: 2x = 14, x = 7, so y = 3. Answer: **x = 7, y = 3**.

summary: Sortable tables with three yes/no or true/false statements.
ideas: You can sort the table by any column; sorting replaces most manual searching.
Each statement is judged on its own, and all three must be right to score.
Typical tasks: counts above a threshold, ranks, medians, ratios between columns, percent of a total.
method: Read the title, column headers and units first.
For each statement, decide which column answers it and sort by that column.
Compute only what the statement needs, and estimate when a clear margin allows it.
traps: Units such as “$ thousands” or percent versus absolute values.
“At least” versus “more than” at the boundary.
Ties in rankings, and the median of an even number of rows.
shortcuts: A ratio across two columns (like revenue per employee) cannot be sorted directly: estimate the few candidates that could win.

summary: Reading charts and completing statements with drop-down menus.
ideas: Charts can be bar, line, scatter, pie or bubble charts, or Venn diagrams.
Each statement has blanks with drop-down choices; read the choices before calculating.
Common tasks: percent change, trend, slope of a line, correlation, share of a total.
method: Read the title, axes, units, scale and legend.
Find exactly what the blank asks for.
Estimate first: the drop-down choices are usually far enough apart.
traps: An axis that does not start at zero exaggerates differences.
Reading the wrong series or the wrong axis.
shortcuts: Round the values you read to easy numbers; exact reading is rarely needed.

example.q: A bar grows from 16 to 20. By what percent did it increase?
example.a: Increase 4 on a base of 16: 4/16 = **25%**. Not 20%: the base is the starting value.

summary: Two or three tabs of text, tables and charts that questions combine.
ideas: Tabs can hold text (emails, reports), tables and charts.
Some questions need one tab, others need two together.
Questions are multiple choice or three yes/no statements.
method: Skim every tab once and note in a few words what each one contains.
For each question, decide which tab or tabs it needs.
Look for conditions, exceptions and rules in text tabs; they often decide the answer.
traps: Missing a condition stated in another tab.
Applying a rule outside the situation it covers.
Reading every tab in detail before seeing the questions.
shortcuts: Keep a short note: tab 1 = policy, tab 2 = costs, tab 3 = schedule.
